question: to the Commission Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Michele Picaro (ECR), Ruggero Razza (ECR) Subject:

In December 2025, the Commission adopted the EU cardiovascular health plan (Safe Hearts Plan). More than half of adults in the EU are overweight and obesity is now one of the main drivers of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and cancer, acting through hypertension, insulin resistance and systemic inflammation. The childhood obesity crisis is accelerating (around 1 in 4 children aged 7 to 9 are overweight and 1 in 10 obese), compounding long-term cardiovascular risk from childhood. In the light of the above: 1.

What specific, educational and binding measures are already provided for in the Safe Hearts Plan and what steps does the Commission plan to take to address the root causes of cardiovascular diseases, in particular obesity and, most importantly, childhood obesity?
Does the Commission agree that obesity is the main cause of heart disease?
What specific action is it planning with a view to addressing obesity and promoting the traditional Mediterranean diet effectively?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) In line with Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU1, the Union complements national policies and encourages cooperation across Member States in the field of public health. Therefore, the Commission is supporting Member States in addressing noncommunicable diseases and their risk factors, including obesity, through the ‘Healthier Together’ initiative2. Actions funded under the EU4Health Programme3 include PreventNCD4, Health4EUkids5 and stakeholder-led projects6, such as PODiaCar7. The Safe Hearts Plan8 builds on these actions for young people under its prevention pillar. Through the aforementioned initiatives, this Plan addresses obesity as one of the main contributing factors in the development of heart disease. The Safe Hearts Plan addresses lifelong prevention, including obesity, through existing actions and those newly funded under the EU4Health work programme, such as a Joint Action on lifelong prevention9 funded with EUR 5 million and supported technically by the World Health Organization and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Two flagships of the Plan specifically address ultra-processed foods, toward healthier diets. The plan makes it clear that the Commission intends to continue to provide EU funding to support physical activity, including its crucial role in prevention, through programmes such as Erasmus10 and EU4Health. Furthermore, obesity is addressed through the Council Recommendation on health-enhancing physical activity11, the European Week of Sport12 and the #BeActive campaign13. The Mediterranean diet is recognised as a model for healthy living in the EU Strategy for Adriatic and Ionian Vision for 203014.
